claims.text: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength in its as-cast solid-solution state.
The relatively low hardness and strength are primarily caused by the absence of nanoscale short-range-order clusters.
Intermediate-temperature annealing promotes the formation of short-range-order clusters in CoCrFeNiTi.
Short-range-order clusters act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
Formation of short-range order will increase the alloy's hardness and strength without compromising favorable plasticity and machinability.
Standard casting of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi produces a homogeneous, disordered solid-solution microstructure.
Annealing at 600 °C for 1–10 hours followed by rapid quenching will lock in the short-range-order state.
The annealing treatment forms nanoscale short-range-order clusters or incipient ordered domains within the disordered matrix.
Short-range-order clusters serve as internal dislocation barriers and pinning points during deformation.
Dislocation pinning by short-range order increases the energy required for dislocation motion.
The increased resistance to dislocation motion enhances hardness and compressive strength while retaining sufficient ductility for machinability.
Annealed and rapidly quenched specimens will have higher yield strength than the as-cast control.
Annealed and rapidly quenched specimens will have higher hardness than the as-cast control.
Short-range-order formation will produce enhanced diffuse scattering in XRD.
Short-range-order formation will be observable as clear nanoscale ordering in TEM.
The annealed specimens will retain relatively high ductility despite their increased strength and hardness.
The as-cast alloy has good plasticity and machinability.
The as-cast alloy's lower hardness and strength result from a lack of dislocation obstacles.
